title: Knowledge and Memory
subtitle: Separate retrieved knowledge, interaction memory, and the current context
summary: Knowledge retrieval supplies information beyond the model’s parameters, while memory preserves useful history from earlier interactions and actions. Neither is the same as the limited context provided to a particular invocation. Lexical retrieval helps with exact names and terms; vector search can find related meanings despite different wording. Graph-based retrieval adds explicit relationships but requires additional construction, validation, and maintenance. Working memory and notes help organize evidence for the current task, while persistent records need selection and updating over time. Choose these mechanisms according to the information the task needs: storing more material does not ensure that the right material reaches the model.

concepts.title: Context windows
concepts.body: An agent’s context window limits what can be supplied to a model invocation. Context engineering decides what to retain, summarize, retrieve, or discard so relevant evidence survives without overwhelming the model.
concepts.example: Teaching extension: A long support conversation is summarized, but the selected order number and unresolved customer request remain explicit. Only the policy passages relevant to that request are added to the next call.

concepts.title: Full-text retrieval
concepts.body: Keyword retrieval such as BM25 finds exact terms and names efficiently. It can miss paraphrases and semantic matches, so ranking, chunking, and query formulation affect what evidence reaches the agent.
concepts.example: Teaching extension: A maintenance assistant searches for the exact fault code E-417 before trying broader descriptive queries, so a similarly worded error for another device does not displace the precise match.

concepts.title: Semantic vectors
concepts.body: Embeddings represent text as dense vectors; nearest-neighbor search retrieves by meaning. It handles paraphrase but can blur precise terms and inherits errors from embedding, chunking, and index choices.
concepts.example: Teaching extension: A user asks how to “stop emails,” and vector retrieval finds an article titled “Disable subscription notifications.” The assistant still checks that the article applies to the current product.

concepts.title: Memory lifecycle
concepts.body: Persistent memory needs explicit rules for what is written, how it is retrieved, when it is updated, and when it is removed. Episodic records of prior interactions serve a different purpose from reusable knowledge or procedures. A memory store can help preserve context across tasks, but stale, incorrect, or irrelevant memories can also propagate mistakes into later decisions.
concepts.example: Teaching extension: A user changes their preferred delivery address. The memory store updates the active preference instead of retrieving both the old and new address as equally current facts.

misconceptions.claim: Context windows is provided automatically by a more capable model.
misconceptions.correction: An agent’s context window limits what can be supplied to a model invocation. Context engineering decides what to retain, summarize, retrieve, or discard so relevant evidence survives without overwhelming the model.

misconceptions.claim: Full-text retrieval removes the need for evaluation or human judgment.
misconceptions.correction: Keyword retrieval such as BM25 finds exact terms and names efficiently. It can miss paraphrases and semantic matches, so ranking, chunking, and query formulation affect what evidence reaches the agent. Evaluation and appropriate oversight remain necessary.

scenario.title: Policy assistant stale memory
scenario.context: An assistant retrieves changing internal policy and also remembers user preferences.

options.label: Keep policy in retrieval and store only durable preferences
options.benefit: Reduces stale authoritative memory and keeps context purposeful.
options.cost: The system needs separate update and deletion rules.
options.consequence: A policy revision appears immediately while a preferred format persists.

options.label: Store all answers in memory
options.cost: Outdated guidance can be repeated with confidence.
options.consequence: A user follows superseded policy and the team must trace the source.

scenario.debrief: Both choices can fit different constraints. The decision should state stakes, reversibility, evidence, and who owns correction.

quiz.question: A policy question depends on an exact product code. Which retrieval method is a useful first fit?
options: Lexical retrieval that preserves the exact identifier.
Similarity search with no exact-match handling.
quiz.explanation: Exact terms often matter for codes; semantic similarity solves a different matching problem.

quiz.question: Why use semantic vector retrieval?
options: Related meanings can match despite different wording.
It guarantees the newest document is selected.
quiz.explanation: Embeddings help match meaning, while freshness, permissions, and relevance checking remain separate concerns.

quiz.question: What makes persistent memory more than an ever-growing transcript?
options: Adding all stored text to every request.
Selection, updating, retrieval, and deletion rules tied to its purpose.
quiz.explanation: Memory needs a lifecycle so useful context can be found without retaining stale or unnecessary material.
